_expect.name: The Crag Next Door - Sport and Trad

on_the_crag_next_door_sport_and_trad.blurb: A modest escarpment cliff in the Burlington and Waterdown corner of the Golden Horseshoe, with mostly sport routes and a handful of trad lines on limestone that is still fairly fresh and unpolished. The wall faces southeast, so trees give a mix of sun and shade, mainly in the morning. Grades run from easy beginner climbs through a solid run of 5.8 to 5.11, with the largest cluster in the 5.12s for people looking to push. It sees fewer climbers than the busier cliffs nearby. Bugs can be heavy in summer, and a stick clip is handy because some of the anchors and first bolts deserve a careful look.
on_the_crag_next_door_sport_and_trad.approach: Faint paths lead to the cliff from either side. The east approach finishes with a steep drop helped by a fixed cord; the west approach has a short downclimb past chains and slings. A V-shaped chimney partway along the wall gives another way down.

on_bon_echo.blurb: Tall trad cliffs that rise straight out of Mazinaw Lake in eastern Ontario, reaching roughly 100 m. Nearly everything here is traditional, much of it multi-pitch with two to four pitches, on cracks, grooves and slabs. Grades start at the very easiest fifth-class and climb through the 5.10s, with a good share between 5.4 and 5.9, so there is plenty for newer leaders as well as harder objectives. Because the wall drops into the water, most parties arrive by boat, which makes planning part of the day. Rock on the popular lines is solid, but less-travelled routes can be loose, so treat them with care.

on_wonderland.blurb: One of the boulder clusters on the floor of the Niagara Glen, a forested gorge beside the Niagara River. The problems are on dolomite blocks that are mostly short, and the grades lean easy: the bulk fall between V0 and V2, with a handful in the V4 to V10 range for stronger climbers. Heavy use has polished the classics, so holds can feel slick and friction matters. Spring and fall give the best conditions. Expect a walk in from the lot, and bring pads, since the landings vary from block to block.
on_wonderland.approach: From the lot, follow the main trail through the park to the metal staircase, go down it, and keep heading north from the bottom; Wonderland sits in that cluster with Central and Bizzaro World.

on_central.blurb: The first boulder cluster most visitors pass on the way into the Niagara Glen, a forested gorge above the Niagara River. The blocks are dolomite, and the problems range widely: easy slab and face climbs at V0 to V2, a solid middle, then a steady line of V5 and V6 problems and a few much harder ones. Some of the best problems are tall, so pad placement and spotters matter. Years of traffic have polished the classics, which can feel nearly frictionless. Spring and fall tend to be the best seasons.
on_central.approach: From the lot, follow the main trail through the park to the metal staircase and go down it. At the bottom continue straight north; Central is the first area you meet.

on_rattlesnake_point_east_cliff.blurb: The eastern stretch of the Rattlesnake Point escarpment, a busy conservation-area cliff close to Toronto that mixes trad leading, sport climbing and top roping. Trad routes outnumber sport here, and grades run from beginner level through the 5.10s and into 5.11, with most routes between 5.3 and 5.10. Bolted anchors along the cliff top make top-rope setups easy, which is why instructors and groups favor it. The popular lines have become polished, and weekends are crowded, so a weekday or early start helps. A helmet is a good idea on the escarpment edge.

on_bottle_glass.blurb: A short piece of escarpment lying between Buffalo Crag and the main wall at Rattlesnake Point, and the one spot there with a good run of sport routes alongside some trad. The rock is less polished than the main wall and the cliff is low, from highball height to a little over a gym wall. Grades are friendly, with the bulk around 5.7 to 5.9 and little beyond 5.11. It catches the sun, which suits early and late in the season, and it is quieter than the main wall though weekends can still be busy. Wear sturdy shoes for the walk because broken glass lies at the base, and bring a stick clip for the high first bolts.
on_bottle_glass.parking_note: Drive into Rattlesnake Point Conservation Area off Appleby Line, north of Burlington, and leave the car in the lower lot.
on_bottle_glass.approach: A short stroll from the trailhead sign at the lower lot, heading south toward the cliff edge. An easy downclimb sits a few metres east of the end of the stone barrier wall.

or_area_51.blurb: A forest crag on the eastern flank of Mt. Hood: a single cliff band of nicely featured andesite about 60 to 70 feet high. Roughly two thirds of the routes are bolted sport lines and the rest are trad, almost all in the 5.9 to 5.12 range with the heaviest concentration at 5.10 and 5.11. A few easier routes exist, but this is mostly a place for intermediate and harder leaders. The crag is split into small sectors, and route names follow an alien and science-fiction theme. It is reached by a forest-road drive and a short trail below the bluff.

or_meadow_camp.blurb: A short basalt cliff band just outside Bend, in national forest beside the Deschutes River. The rock is 20 to 40 feet tall and offers vertical cracks, corners and faces, with a mix of delicate and physical moves. It is mostly top-rope and trad climbing, with no sport bolts, plus a few boulder problems at the base and downstream. Grades run from 5.6 up to 5.12, with the biggest group at 5.9. Shade from big pines helps a few climbs, but summer afternoons can be hot, so spring and fall are more comfortable. The setting is quiet and often secluded.
or_meadow_camp.parking_note: Leave Bend on the Cascade Lakes road and bear onto a gravel track shortly before the golf course; about a mile along it ends at a lot beside the river.
or_meadow_camp.approach: Walk downstream a couple of hundred feet from the lot to the climbers' path that climbs to the base of the cliff.
